title: Skip entry — surfing back out of the atmosphere
intro_sentence: Too fast for a single dip, the capsule skips back out of the atmosphere, coasts, then re-enters — splitting a brutal heat load into two gentler bites.
narrative_101: Something falling back from low Earth orbit arrives at about 7.8 kilometres a second. Something falling back from the Moon arrives at nearly 11 km/s. That extra speed is a huge amount of extra energy, all of which has to become heat, and dumping it all in one pass would overwhelm the heat shield and slam the crew with too many g. So the fastest returns do something that sounds like a mistake: they deliberately skip.

The capsule dips into the upper atmosphere, uses its lift to bleed off just enough speed, then pulls back up and coasts — briefly — back above the sensible air, a long ballistic arc through near-vacuum, before dropping in a second time for the final descent. It is the same physics as skipping a stone across water, except the goal is not to stay up but to spread the punishment of re-entry across two gentler bites instead of one savage one.

Apollo did not need to skip, but the uncrewed Soviet Zond probes (Zond 6 and 7) demonstrated a double-dip guided entry, China’s Chang’e 5 sample-return skipped to bleed off lunar-return speed over Inner Mongolia, and NASA’s Orion flies a skip-guidance entry on Artemis — the skip also stretches the reachable range by thousands of kilometres, letting the capsule wait out the energy and come down near the recovery fleet.
body_paragraphs: A skip entry is practical only above the speed of a circular orbit at that altitude (~7.9 km/s low down) — a "super-circular" return. During the first dip the vehicle uses lift-up to arrest the descent before it has slowed all the way down; with energy still above what a closed orbit at that altitude needs, the trajectory carries it back up out of the sensible atmosphere. It then follows an exo-atmospheric coast — energy conserved, no drag — until it falls back for the second, final entry.

The payoff is threefold. Peak heating and peak deceleration are lower because the total energy is shed in two passes rather than one. The reachable downrange grows dramatically — the coast between dips can span thousands of kilometres — which lets mission planners target a specific recovery zone from a wide range of arrival conditions. And the thermal soak is split, easing the heat-shield’s job.

The cost is guidance difficulty: the vehicle must judge the first dip precisely, because too little energy bled and it skips too high or fails to come back down usefully, too much and it never leaves the atmosphere. Modern skip guidance (as on Orion) solves this in closed loop, modulating bank angle through the first entry to place the exit conditions — and therefore the second entry and the landing point — exactly where they need to be.
diagram_caption: Super-circular skip: a first atmospheric dip bleeds energy, the vehicle climbs back into an exo-atmospheric coast, then re-enters — two gentle bites instead of one, and thousands of km more range.
